'''Eugenie Maria Morenus''' (February 21, 1881 – October 15, 1966) was an American mathematician and college professor and one of the few women to earn a PhD in math before World War II. She taught Latin and mathematics at [[Sweet Briar College]] from 1909 to 1946.

== Early life and education ==
Morenus was born in [[Cleveland, New York]], the daughter of Eugene Morenus and Maria Euphemia Van Blarcom Morenus.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Daughters of the American Revolution|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jO4QAQAAMAAJ&q=Eugenie+Morenus&pg=PA22|title=Lineage Book|date=1917|publisher=The Society|pages=22|language=en}}</ref> Her father managed a glassworks. She graduated from [[Monongahela, Pennsylvania|Monogahela High School]] in 1898.<ref>{{Cite news|date=1898-06-02|title=The School Exhibition|pages=1|work=The Daily Republican|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/73664023/the-school-exhibition/|access-date=2021-03-17|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> She earned a bachelor's degree from [[Vassar College]] in 1904, and a master's degree from the same school in 1905.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last1=Green|first1=Judy|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=IRbOAwAAQBAJ&q=Eugenie+Morenus&pg=PA252|title=Pioneering Women in American Mathematics: The Pre-1940 PhD's|last2=LaDuke|first2=Jeanne|date=2009|publisher=American Mathematical Soc.|isbn=978-0-8218-4376-5|pages=252–253|language=en}}</ref> She completed doctoral studies in mathematics at [[Columbia University]] in 1922. Her dissertation under [[Edward Kasner]] was titled "Geometric properties completely characterizing the set of all the curves of constant pressure in a field of force".<ref>[https://www.genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu/id.php?id=37359 Eugenie Maria Morenus], Mathematics Genealogy Project, North Dakota State University.</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Morenus|first=Eugenie M.|url=https://catalog.hathitrust.org/Record/000385756|title=Geometric properties completely characterizing the set of all the curves of constant pressure in a field of force / by Eugenie M. Morenus.|date=1922|publisher=Press of the John C. Winston Co.|location=Philadelphia}}</ref>

Morenus was also a student for briefer periods at the [[University of Chicago]], and at [[Göttingen Academy of Sciences and Humanities|Göttingen]].<ref>{{Cite book|last=Singer|first=Sandra L.|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7Llyixb94lcC&q=Eugenie+Morenus&pg=PA95|title=Adventures Abroad: North American Women at German-speaking Universities, 1868-1915|date=2003|publisher=Greenwood Publishing Group|isbn=978-0-313-32371-3|pages=95|language=en}}</ref> 

== Career ==
Morenus taught mathematics and Latin at a school in [[Watertown (city), New York|Watertown, New York]] and at [[Poughkeepsie High School]] after her master's degree.<ref name=":0" /> She was a Latin instructor at Sweet Briar College from 1909 to 1916, and was a mathematics professor at the same school from 1916 to 1946.<ref>{{Cite news|date=1956-01-29|title=Golden Anniversary Celebration Set|pages=43|work=The Times Dispatch|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/73661748/golden-anniversary-celebration-set/|access-date=2021-03-17|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|date=1922|title=Notes and News|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2972833|journal=The American Mathematical Monthly|volume=29|issue=2|pages=93–96|doi=10.1080/00029890.1922.11986108|jstor=2972833|issn=0002-9890}}</ref> She was head of the mathematics department for much of that time. While at the school she was prominent in campus events, as a chorister, photographer, and play director. Her horse, October or "Toby", was a familiar figure on campus, and Morenus would lead ten-day rides for students over spring breaks.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Poleski|first=Dana|date=2020-12-22|title=100 Years of Equestrian Excellence|url=https://sbc.edu/news/100-years-of-equestrian-excellence/|access-date=2021-03-17|website=Sweet Briar College {{!}} News|language=en-US}}</ref>

Morenus was a charter member of the [[Mathematical Association of America]], belonged to the [[Virginia Academy of Science]], and was active in the [[American Association of University Women]] (AAUW).<ref name=":0" /> She was active in the [[Order of the Eastern Star]] and the [[Daughters of the American Revolution]].<ref>{{Cite news|date=1966-10-20|title=Obituaries: Miss Eugenie Morenus|pages=119|work=The Orlando Sentinel|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/73661984/obituaries-miss-eugenie-morenus/|access-date=2021-03-17|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> She received an [[Anna Brackett]] Fellowship by the AAUW in 1927, to study at [[University of Cambridge|Cambridge]].<ref>{{Cite news|last=Haskin|first=Frederic J.|date=1927-03-30|title=The Haskin Letter: University Women Meet|pages=4|work=The Independent-Record|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/73663811/the-haskin-letter-university-women/|access-date=2021-03-17|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|date=1927-03-21|title=Eugenie M. Morenus|pages=1|work=The San Francisco Examiner|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/73664272/eugenie-m-morenus/|access-date=2021-03-17|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> After her retirement from Sweet Briar College in 1946, she taught briefly at Connecticut College for Women, and spent her winters in Florida.<ref name=":0" />

== Personal life ==
Morenus died in [[Lake Wales, Florida]] in 1966, aged 85 years.<ref>{{Cite news|date=1966-10-20|title=Morenus|pages=9|work=The Post-Standard|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/73661445/morenus/|access-date=2021-03-17|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|date=1966-10-19|title=Miss Morenus, Ex-Teacher, Dies|pages=29|work=The Post-Standard|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/73661595/miss-morenus-ex-teacher-dies/|access-date=2021-03-17|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> There was a scholarship endowment fund named for Morenus at Sweet Briar College, beginning in 1960.<ref name=":0" />
